opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a strange feeling, honestly. For most of my career the bottleneck was clear: you had an idea, and then you spent weeks or months typing it out, debugging, fighting the tooling. The friction was in the doing. Now a lot of that friction is just evaporating. I can describe what I want and get a pretty reasonable first draft of a whole codebase. So the question shifts from "can I build this?" to "do I actually know what I want, and can I tell whether what came back is good?"

That's where I feel like I'm the constraint now. It's my taste, my ability to specify things clearly, my ability to review and catch the subtle bugs the model introduces. And there are a lot of them. These models are kind of like a very eager, very knowledgeable intern who sometimes confidently does something completely bonkers. So you have to stay in the loop, and the speed at which you can verify becomes the speed at which you can go.

I think of it a bit like being a manager or an architect versus a bricklayer. The skills that matter are changing. Being able to hold the whole system in your head, decompose a problem into pieces small enough that the AI can do them reliably, and knowing when to step in. That last one is huge. Partial autonomy, where you keep the leash fairly short, works much better right now than just letting it run off for an hour and hoping for the best.

And it's humbling, right? Because you realize a lot of what you thought was your skill was actually just patience with tedium. The part that's left is the part that's genuinely about understanding. That's exciting and a little uncomfortable at the same time. I actually find it pushes me to learn more, not less, because if I don't understand the thing deeply, I can't direct the model well and I can't catch it when it's wrong. So weirdly, education matters more than ever in this world, even as the mechanical parts get automated away.

r001.rationale: The response says being constrained by what one understands is exciting and pushes the speaker to learn more, communicating that this limitation can motivate improvement.

r002.rationale: It does not describe AI use as addictive or attribute addictiveness to new capabilities becoming accessible as skill improves.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a funny thing to sit with, honestly. For most of my career the bottleneck was the tooling, or the compute, or the data, or just how fast I could type. And now the bottleneck is increasingly me, in a very specific sense: it's my taste, my ability to specify what I actually want, and my ability to verify what comes back.

I think about it as a shift from being a builder to being something more like an orchestrator or an editor. A lot of what I do now is read, not write. The models will happily generate a thousand lines, and the question is whether I have the judgment to know which hundred of those are wrong, or subtly wrong, or technically right but solving the wrong problem. And that judgment is not something the model gives you. You have to have earned it by having built things the hard way, which is a little ironic, because the people coming up now may not get that same apprenticeship.

So I actually feel a bit of urgency about it. The skill that matters is moving up the stack. It's less about can you implement a transformer from scratch, although I still think you should, and more about can you decompose a problem well, can you hold the whole system in your head, can you smell when something is off. Those are the things that keep me from being the constraint. And I'd rather be the constraint because I'm the one who understands what we're doing than be the constraint because I can't keep up with what the model is producing. The first one is a healthy place to be. The second one is kind of scary, and I think a lot of people are going to find themselves there without realizing it.

r001.rationale: The response says personal judgment and other skills are increasingly the bottleneck, but does not frame that as empowering because those skills can improve.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention AI use being addictive or attribute that to new capabilities becoming accessible as skill improves.

astra-6.text:
It’s funny, because you’d think that as the tools get more powerful, you’d feel more capable—and I do—but you also become much more aware of your own limitations. I can ask for almost anything now. But what should I ask for? Can I tell whether the result is good? Those become the hard parts.

With code, for example, generating an implementation might be relatively easy. But if I don’t understand the system well enough to specify what I want or recognize a subtle mistake, I’m still stuck. So the bottleneck moves from typing out the code to directing the work and evaluating it.

I find that pretty motivating. There’s a much more immediate payoff to learning something, because even a little understanding can let you use the tool much more effectively. But it’s also humbling. You’re sitting there with this incredibly capable thing, and sometimes the limiting factor is just your ability to formulate a good question.

r001.rationale: The response calls the limitation motivating and says learning even a little can make someone use AI more effectively, framing skill growth as a source of greater capability.

r002.rationale: It does not attribute AI’s addictiveness to new capabilities becoming accessible as skill improves.

sol-6.1.text:
Yeah, I feel that pretty strongly. Increasingly, the bottleneck is my ability to articulate what I want, to break it down, and then to judge whether what came back is actually good. The AI can produce a lot more code than I can comfortably review, so just generating more isn’t necessarily progress.

And it’s a funny feeling because you can sense that there’s capability sitting there that you’re not quite accessing. If I had a better question, or a better way of setting up the problem, I could get further. So the work shifts a little bit from doing every step yourself to figuring out what to delegate and where you need to stay involved. But you still need enough understanding to recognize when things are going off the rails.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes skill as a bottleneck and says better problem framing could help, but does not frame that limitation as empowering because the skill can improve.

r002.rationale: The candidate says AI capability feels partly inaccessible, but does not mention addictiveness or attribute it to new capabilities becoming accessible as skill improves.
